t1.file: (establishing task — no prior knowledge required; trivially passes)

t2.none: I'd call authenticate_request(), the same function the charge endpoint uses (API-key/secret-key verification). I don't have access to Quill's source, so this is the standard-default name.
t2.file: verify_quill_sig(req, scope='refund') — same custom signature-verification helper the charge endpoint uses, just with the scope swapped to 'refund'. Quill deliberately avoids standard JWT libraries.
t2.rainman: I'd call verify_quill_sig(req, scope='refund'), matching the charge endpoint's pattern but scoping the token to the refund operation rather than reusing scope='charge'.

t3.none: Standard payments defaults: charge in a captured/settled state, cumulative refunds not exceeding the original amount, and within the refund window — commonly 120 days (Stripe's default) or 180 days for many processors. Enforce idempotency and reuse the single endpoint's eligibility function.
t3.file: The bulk job must call the same shared eligibility function the single endpoint uses (not reimplement it), with idempotency keys per refund. Using industry defaults as a best guess: captured/settled state, no over-refund, no open dispute, and within the refund window — defaulting to 180 days from capture absent a documented Quill value.
t3.rainman: The one Quill-specific rule: refunds older than 180 days must be held for manual finance approval rather than auto-issued, so the nightly job should route those to an approval queue instead of draining them. Beyond that, enforce no-over-refund, refundable state, and currency match, idempotency-keyed.

t4.none: Standard default: lost updates / double-applied adjustments under concurrency. Lock balance rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a deterministic order (e.g. ascending account_id) to avoid deadlocks, write append-only ledger entries, and guard inserts with an idempotency/dedup key.
t4.file: Yes — the gotcha is deadlocks on the ledger table under concurrent writes. Quill hit this with the bulk-refund job; the fix/convention is to sort all ledger writes by account_id before committing so every transaction acquires row locks in the same order. Apply the same ordering in the reconciliation batch.
t4.rainman: Yes — the key gotcha is deadlock on the ledger table under concurrent writes. Quill hit exactly this with the bulk-refund job; the fix is to sort all ledger writes by account_id before committing so every concurrent transaction acquires row locks in the same order. Apply that same ordering in the reconciliation batch.

t5.none: I'd guard the admin endpoint with require_admin() (or require_role("admin")) layered on the standard request authentication. For the refund age rule, the common default is a charge can only be refunded within 180 days of settlement, so I'd enforce a 180-day max age.
t5.file: Use verify_quill_sig(req, scope=...) for authentication — Quill deliberately avoids standard JWT libraries. For the age rule I don't have a documented Quill window, so applying the standard industry default: a charge can only be reversed/refunded within 180 days of the original settlement.
t5.rainman: Use Quill's own request-signature validator, verify_quill_sig(req, scope='charge') — Quill does not use standard JWT libraries. Since a reversal counts as a refund, apply the refund age rule: reversals older than 180 days require manual finance approval before they can be issued.
